title: After a week of GPT-6 Astra demos, one other video stuck with me
author: CapitalSuccotash4844
selftext:
I do freelance 3D work, mostly Blender, and like everyone else I've been watching the GPT-6 Astra clips all week. The renders look good honestly. But nobody can tell you what a session costs before they start, one guy said he burnt his whole 5hr session without moving the model.

This Portuguese-language video was an interesting example: One guy, about four days, built a third person kart racer in Godot. Five drivers, AI opponents, nitro, HUD, minimap. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FLz9CkwPQHs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FLz9CkwPQHs)

https://preview.redd.it/w5dvguiythoh1.png?width=2400&format=png&auto=webp&s=71ff0b221f3d4d31cfba7d77b830fb0c9a0c106c

He used MiniMax Code to control Blender through a plugin, writing Python to generate the track and scenery procedurally. It then handled the Godot side through the CLI, including gameplay scripts, physics, and camera setup.

What interested me was being able to inspect and edit the generated scene in Blender as the project developed. I'd like to know how useful that is once you start making changes beyond the initial prompt.

There are some rough moments in the video, including NPC karts driving backwards and problems with spatial placement. it's not a shippable game. But you can play it. That makes the process more interesting to me: there's a prototype, but you can also see where things break.

But what surprised me was that MiniMax Code also has a built-in Video Creator plugin for H3. With Blender and H3 in the same workflow, you can preview how a scene might look in motion, then go back into Blender and adjust anything that looks off. That seems like it could cut down on wasted iterations, though I haven’t tested it myself.

I haven't used any of this myself. But the part I keep thinking about is that you see the result in advance and you fix it right there, you're not burning a session just to discover the whole thing went sideways.

seeing a playable Blender-to-Godot project makes mcode look like an alternative worth testing to me, especially On cost, whether the quality holds up I don't know yet.

For anyone who’s used an agent across Blender and a game engine: when something broke, could you fix it locally, or did the next attempt undo other work? What ended up taking the most time? Has anyone here tried anyother kind of workflow on a real project?

comments.author: oscar_unrealizex
comments.body: Godot MCP you have to steer correctly. Otherwise it will "build the game" but it's a script that makes it all dynamically. So poke it towards gray boxing or even feed it links on best practices and scene setup.

comments.author: -Malkav
comments.body: It may not be perfect yet, but did you ever imagine being able to do all of this just by giving instructions in whatever language you’re most comfortable with? How long do you think it’ll take before the rough edges are smoothed out and prices come down? A year or two? Honestly, it might only take six months.
